results.content: # Coherent Bayesian Regularization Methods in Measurement Invariance Evaluation. ##### Add to collection. *You do not have access to any existing collections. You may create a new collection.*. ## Downloadable Content. Request Version for Screen Reader. #### Citation. #### MLA. *Coherent Bayesian Regularization Methods In Measurement Invariance Evaluation.* 2021. #### APA. *Coherent Bayesian Regularization Methods in Measurement Invariance Evaluation.*. #### Chicago. *Coherent Bayesian Regularization Methods In Measurement Invariance Evaluation.*. + College of Arts and Sciences, Department of Psychology and Neuroscience. : * Psychological studies that involve heterogeneous groups need to evaluate scale items and account for any differential item performance in reflecting the underlying constructs. Classical methods to evaluate differential item functioning (DIF) require an anchor item set that remains invariant across groups, yet these methods tend to incur inflated error rates when the anchor item assumption is incorrect. Recent approaches use lasso regularization to simultaneously detect DIF in all items and avoid incorrect anchor item assumptions. Although promising, lasso methods cause other inferential issues such as invalid standard errors and incorrect p-values for regularized estimates. An effective alternative may be Bayesian regularization, which separates variable selection from estimate shrinkage. However, it remains unclear how to choose among various empirical Bayesian variable selection criteria in the DIF detection context. This study clarifies the limitations of empirical Bayesian variable selection criteria. We argue that a spike-and-slab prior with an inclusion probability criterion provides more theoretically coherent DIF selection over other empirical selection rules. We conducted simulation studies with item response theory (IRT) and moderated nonlinear factor analysis (MNLFA) models to demonstrate the advantageous DIF selection performance of the spike-and-slab prior selection rule in comparison to other Bayesian regularizing priors and frequentist lasso. We also compared inferential quality of these DIF selection models and provided practical recommendations for using the spike-and-slab prior rule in measurement invariance evaluation. : * In Copyright - Educational Use Permitted. : * University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Graduate School. ## Relations. results.content: # Differential Item Functioning (DIF). Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when test items perform differently for subgroups of equal ability, potentially indicating test bias. DIF analysis identifies items that unfairly advantage or disadvantage specific demographic groups, ensuring test fairness and validity across diverse populations. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is a statistical property of test items that occurs when individuals from different groups (such as gender, ethnicity, or language background) with the same underlying ability level have different probabilities of answering an item correctly. DIF provides a framework for identifying and addressing such bias at the item level, distinguishing it from legitimate group differences in the construct being measured. * Understand the distinction between DIF and item bias. * Learn major statistical methods for DIF detection. * Recognize the implications of DIF for test validity and fairness. Uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups remains constant across all ability levels. For example, if an item consistently favors one group by the same amount regardless of ability level, it exhibits uniform DIF. Non-uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups varies across ability levels. This method can detect both uniform and non-uniform DIF through hierarchical model comparison. IRT-based DIF detection compares item parameters across groups, examining differences in difficulty, discrimination, and guessing parameters. This approach addresses the contamination problem where DIF items affect the matching variable, providing more accurate detection especially when multiple items exhibit DIF. When examining DIF across multiple groups simultaneously, methods include generalized Mantel-Haenszel statistics, multiple indicator multiple cause (MIMIC) models, and multi-group IRT approaches. Bundle DIF examines differential functioning at the testlet or subscale level rather than individual items. Bundle DIF can reveal systematic bias patterns that individual item analysis might miss. DIF analysis informs item writing and revision processes. Items flagged for DIF undergo content review to identify potential sources of bias, such as culturally specific references, gendered language, or differential curricular exposure. DIF analysis provides empirical evidence for test fairness, supporting legal defensibility under employment and educational testing guidelines. In international testing programs, DIF analysis identifies items that function differently across countries or languages. A handbook on the theory and methods of differential item functioning (DIF).

This blog post explores the concept of Differential Item Functioning (DIF) and its role in ensuring fairness in testing. We will also discuss the results of DIF analysis of TestGorilla tests and how they can help in creating more equitable assessment methods. One effective tool for this purpose is **Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis**. To achieve such fairness in testing, it is crucial to ensure that every test item accurately and equitably measures the intended construct across all groups of test-takers. DIF is employed to rigorously evaluate whether individual test items function differently for distinct groups, even when those groups possess equivalent levels of the ability being measured. DIF analysis is a sophisticated and reliable method for identifying biased test items. Rather than simply removing questions that show large differences in average scores between groups, DIF analysis compares how different groups (such as a male and a female) perform on each test item. DIF analysis has been effectively used to detect biased items and is recommended for high-stakes assessments *(Martinková et al., 2017)*. However, this item could be a potential source of gender DIF. Identifying the sources of gender-based Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is crucial for developing fair and unbiased tests. results.title: 7 Key Insights on Noninformative Priors in Bayesian Methods
results.content: # 7 Key Insights on Noninformative Priors in Bayesian Methods 7 Key Insights on Noninformative Priors in Bayesian Methods Bayesian statistics has long transformed how we approach statistical modeling, inference, and decision-making. > **Discover essential insights behind noninformative priors in Bayesian analysis.** > Learn how these impartial frameworks shape inference and statistical modeling effectively. With noninformative priors, even with limited data, the conclusion strives to remain as unbiased as possible, thus reflecting more accurately the information content in the data itself. ### Advantages and Potential Pitfalls The use of noninformative priors in Bayesian analysis offers several clear advantages: When explicit prior knowledge is unreliable or unavailable, noninformative priors allow for an analysis that is as driven by the data as possible, thereby enhancing the objectivity of the results. When comparing models, noninformative priors help ensure that differences in the conclusions are primarily due to the data and not because of strong prior assumptions. ## Applications in Bayesian Analysis The real utility of noninformative priors is most evident when applied to a diverse range of statistical modeling scenarios. When little prior information is available about β0​ and β1​, noninformative priors such as This ensures that the posterior inference is determined predominantly by the observed data, leading to a robust evaluation of model parameters. 3. **Survival Analysis and Reliability:** In survival analysis, crucial parameters like the baseline hazard rate might be modeled with noninformative priors to avoid assumptions about the underlying distribution. ### Case Studies Demonstrating Impact Several case studies have successfully illustrated the merits of employing noninformative priors in Bayesian methods: Consider the challenge of modeling pollutant levels in a river where background data is limited. ### Comparative Analysis with Other Methods When comparing noninformative priors with other forms of priors, the differences become starkly apparent: Informative priors can potentially reduce variance in the posterior estimates but at the expense of introducing bias, particularly problematic when prior assumptions do not hold true. By employing noninformative priors, researchers can pursue more data-driven conclusions without the sway of possibly unsound or overly specific assumptions inherent in informative priors. By carefully considering the definition, core assumptions, inherent advantages, and practical limitations of noninformative priors, researchers can design Bayesian models that aspire to objective, data-driven inference.
